newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pledges reforms but no stock market bailout.
newsitem.headline: Japan pledges reforms but no stock market bailout.

text.p: Japanese authorities on Friday sought to stem the Tokyo stock market plunge with calls for calm and renewed promises of economic reform, but warned the market not to expect a government bailout.
And economists said that for now, officialdom looked unlikely to ride to the rescue.

The market's key barometer, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, plunged another 4.26 percent to 17,303.65 on Friday, continuing the downward spiral that began late last year on worries about the economic outlook, the pace of structural reforms and the health of financial firms.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka sought to ease market fears, urging calm and promising to carry out proposed financial and other economic reforms.
"Financial markets move on varying factors and it is important to stay calm," Mitsuzuka told a news conference. "We are determined to carry out reforms steadily and without fail."
He also repeated the official view that the economy was gradually recovering and urged firms to have confidence.
Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso, meanwhile, warned the stock market not to expect a government bailout.
"Prices can only be determined by the market," Aso told a separate news conference. "It's not for the government to interfere."
Vague rumours that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto might cut short a Southeast Asian tour to deal with the share price plunge were denied by Japanese diplomats in Tokyo and Jakarta.
Market pundits have cited a raft of reasons -- some of them contradictory -- for the steep decline.

Among the oft-cited causes are growing concerns that the government's fiscal tightening, aimed at getting its big budget deficit under control, could stall the economic recovery, and fears that planned deregulation could hurt financial firms long accustomed to a protected environment.
Snowballing public debt and dwindling tax revenues during Japan's economic slump have made its budget deficit worse than those of other major industrial nations.

Somewhat perversely, however, analysts also cite a belief that Japan's proposed economic restructuring will be too slow to help the economy regain its competitive edge as a key factor behind the share market slump.
"Don't ask me to rationalise the stock market, because I don't think the market is rational. It's become a herd," said one economist. "It's one of those vicious cycles."

Economists' prescriptions for remedies the government ought to pursue varied according to their preferred explanation for the fall. Among the proposals are postponing a sales tax increase due to go into effect from April 1, redrafting the budget to attack spending aimed at pleasing special interests, and standing firm while market forces take their course.
Many agreed, however, that officials were unlikely to shift policy gears unless the Nikkei neared the 15,000 level -- and perhaps not even then.
"To be honest, obviously to everyone in the financial sector it's a big problem, but maybe it's not such a big problem for the economy," said ING Baring Securities chief economist Richard Jerram.

Analysts say that if the Nikkei hit around 15,000, banks' unrealised profits on shareholdings would evaporate, eroding their ability to tackle the remaining legacy of bad debts after the collapse of Japan's 1980s asset bubble.

"Normally, when the market was down before, there was some policy move to rescue it, but so far the government is saying 'not this time'," said Peter Morgan, a senior economist at James Capel Pacific. "The market is having to go cold turkey (abruptly end a habit)."
Others, however, said Hashimoto's conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) might have to make some gesture towards looser fiscal policy in response to market demands.
"I think the LDP cannot afford to ignore the market's demands," said Takashi Kiuchi, head of economic research at LTCB Research Institute.
